r: Introduction to Human Services surveys the profession broadly — theories, models, programs, best practices, and populations served — much of which is content delivery and synthesis that maps to Getting Information and Interpreting Information rather than applied clinical judgment. Observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical and writing/office tasks dominate current AI use, and a survey-style course like this could plausibly draw on AI-generated summaries of service models or agency comparisons. Even so, realized classroom adoption at 24 months remains limited given diffusion research showing only a minority of firms have integrated AI meaningfully, and introductory instruction on professional attitudes and values still leans on instructor framing. The course's General Studies: Social and Behavioral Sciences and GT-SS3 designation binds it into the gtPathways transfer core regardless of how automatable its survey content becomes, keeping the near-term rating Low despite the course's more information-dense character than the sociocultural-critique-heavy education courses.

By five years, more of this course's survey content — summarizing service-delivery models, comparing agency structures, outlining professional-values frameworks — becomes plausible territory for AI-assisted instruction and study support, consistent with capability trends showing steadily longer, more coherent task completion (METR/Epoch doubling estimates). Verification burden stays moderate rather than protective: an introductory overview carries lower error cost than direct client-facing practice, so this factor does not dampen the rating. The course remains fully classroom/digital in delivery with no clinical or field component built into HSP 1010 itself, further removing an embodiment-based floor. The binding constraint at this horizon is institutional rather than task-based: its general-studies and GT-SS3 designation keeps it locked into the gtPathways gen-ed transfer core, capping the rating at Medium even as underlying survey-style content becomes more AI-tractable. This is a plausible trajectory, not a certainty, given how unevenly instructional AI adoption has diffused so far.

A decade out, projecting exactly how much of an introductory survey course's content generation shifts to AI is speculative, though the direction is plausible: broad overviews of professions, theories, and populations are precisely the kind of information-synthesis task that GDPval-style evaluations show current models already handling at a level approaching, if not matching, human expert output. Whether this translates into curricular change is a separate, harder question, since introductory courses also carry socialization and professional-identity functions that resist pure information substitution. What is not speculative is the institutional floor: the general-studies and GT-SS3 designation keeps HSP 1010 anchored in the gtPathways transfer core, a structural requirement unaffected by task-level automation progress, which caps this course at Medium rather than allowing drift toward High. Given the compounding uncertainty over a ten-year window, Medium is offered as a calibrated estimate rather than a firm prediction.
HSP 1010.d: Students receive an overview of the Human Services profession. Students examine the attitudes, values, and skills crucial for becoming effective Human Services professionals. Understanding and working with various populations and cultural groups are essential for those working in Human Services. Students will examine various types of human service theories, models, programs, and current best practices. Students will also survey a variety of client populations and agencies.

That conceptual framing makes it somewhat more tractable to AI-assisted content delivery than a skills-based practicum, but sensitivity around trauma and PTSD populations still carries real error cost if a model oversimplifies safety-oriented practice guidance, consistent with jagged-frontier findings that mis-calibrated trust on nuanced material produces confident errors. Realized 24-month adoption in this kind of introductory human-services instruction remains limited per diffusion data. The course's General Studies: Social and Behavioral Sciences designation locks it into the gtPathways gen-ed transfer core independent of these task-level considerations, holding the near-term rating to Low.

At five years, more of this course's conceptual content — defining TIC frameworks, cataloguing agency-level safety modifications, outlining trauma-informed approaches across populations — plausibly becomes AI-assisted study and instructional material, especially since the course explicitly stops short of clinical intervention training and stays in the descriptive/conceptual register that current writing-and-synthesis-capable models handle reasonably well. Productivity research on professional writing tasks shows meaningful quality and speed gains from AI assistance, which could extend to structuring this kind of conceptual coursework. Verification burden remains moderate rather than strongly protective given the course's non-clinical scope, and delivery stays fully digital with no embodied practicum component. The binding constraint continues to be the General Studies: Social and Behavioral Sciences designation, which anchors the course inside the gtPathways transfer core and caps the rating at Medium regardless of how far task-level automatability advances by this horizon.

Forecasting a full decade for an introductory, non-clinical conceptual course is inherently uncertain — model capability could plausibly handle most descriptive trauma-informed-care content, or human-services programs could deliberately preserve instructor-led delivery for material touching vulnerable populations regardless of technical feasibility, given how the jagged-frontier literature documents costly overconfidence when users lean on AI outside well-verified domains. Diffusion research indicates capability and actual classroom adoption move on different timelines, and nothing about this course signals it would be an early adopter. What remains stable across the uncertainty is the institutional layer: the General Studies: Social and Behavioral Sciences designation ties HSP 1020 into the gtPathways gen-ed transfer core, a structural requirement that persists independent of how the automation question resolves. That designation caps the rating at Medium rather than High, and Medium is offered here as a calibrated hedge rather than a confident ten-year point estimate.
HSP 1020.d: Students will be introduced to the concept of Trauma- Informed Care (TIC) and how agencies and Human Services professionals can utilize this model to benefit clients. Students will describe and define what TIC is and ways in which a traditional treatment setting can be modified to increase the sense of safety experienced by clients and those who work with them. Students will learn how to incorporate trauma-informed practices into treatment with diverse populations, especially those with Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). Although trauma treatment approaches will be considered, this class will not teach how to intervene using trauma specific treatment.

r: HSP 1470 examines addictive lifestyles and experiences through theories of addiction and works toward developing healthy, non-addictive habits, a broad-appeal survey and personal-development course rather than a clinical-skills or licensure-track requirement. The applied work is explanatory and reflective: summarizing addiction theory, discussing habit formation, and writing about personal behavior change, tasks that map closely to updating-and-using-relevant-knowledge and interpreting-information activities that observed-usage data show AI already handles fluently, alongside general writing tasks. Unlike the program's field-gating courses, HSP 1470 carries no prerequisite chain into Practicum I and no GT-Pathways designation, leaving a comparatively weak institutional anchor. At 24 months the instrumental case is already softening: AI can explain addiction theory and draft habit-change frameworks competently, though classroom discussion and personal reflection still give students reasons to engage the material directly.

By 2031, AI will draft addiction-theory summaries, habit-change plans, and reflective writing with real fluency, precisely the kind of explanatory and writing-heavy task that controlled productivity studies show benefits substantially from AI assistance, and that task-exposure research ranks among the most automatable categories. Because the course lacks a hard prerequisite role or accreditation-credit floor tying it to the professional sequence, there is little institutional counterweight to that exposure. The instrumental case for a student personally producing this content weakens meaningfully; AI can generate defensible addiction-theory analysis and personalized habit plans on demand. The rating rises to High, reflecting genuine erosion in both the informational and reflective-writing components, tempered only by the residual value of guided in-class discussion that a generic AI summary does not replicate.

A decade out, AI's capacity to explain addiction science, generate individualized habit-change strategies, and produce reflective analysis will be extensive under a central-case capability trajectory, and nothing in the course's structure, no licensure gate, no accreditation-credit floor, no prerequisite chain, resists that erosion. The instrumental rationale for a dedicated course built around content AI increasingly generates on demand is substantially weakened. The genuine uncertainty concerns whether the course persists as a general-interest elective valued for discussion and community rather than for content transmission, which this rating framework does not credit. Based on the applied-task profile and the absence of binding institutional constraints, the rating holds High, with the caveat that enrollment and intrinsic-value questions, explicitly outside this rating, may diverge sharply from the instrumental-task conclusion.
HSP 1470.d: In this class, students will examine addictive lifestyles and experiences in contemporary America in the context of theories of addiction. In addition, they will focus on the process of developing healthy habits and non-addictive lifestyles.

But the course is one of two required alternatives, with HSP 2020, gating entry to Practicum I, making it load-bearing prerequisite substrate within the accredited program's sequence. Engaging directly with a real organization, gathering firsthand information, evaluating its actual impact, also involves judgment AI cannot exercise on the student's behalf. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: AI can help draft the report, but it does not substitute for the required course credential or the organizational-assessment competence it builds.

By 2031, AI research and drafting tools will more capably synthesize organizational information and produce polished impact reports, eroding the execution rationale for the writing-heavy portion of the assignment. The residual competence is evaluative: assessing whether an AI-assisted analysis of a real nonprofit's impact is accurate, given that jagged-frontier evidence shows AI users can be confidently wrong outside familiar domains. As a required alternative feeding Practicum I, the course's prerequisite role does not relax within a catalog cycle, and foundational scaffolding for the practicum pathway caps how far the rating can fall. The instrumental case shifts toward directing and verifying AI-assisted organizational research rather than performing it manually. The rating holds Low, anchored by the practicum-gating requirement even as the underlying report-writing task grows more automatable.

A decade out, AI-generated organizational analysis and impact reporting will likely be routine and highly capable under a central-case trajectory, substantially eroding the write-the-report-yourself rationale that originally anchors the assignment's design. But HSP 2010 remains foundational scaffolding, a required alternative prerequisite for Practicum I, and that programmatic role persists absent a restructuring of the field-placement sequence, which changes slowly relative to model capability. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting genuine erosion in the applied research-and-writing task while the prerequisite architecture keeps the course firmly in place. The open question is whether the assignment gets redesigned around AI-assisted research, not whether some course preparing students to evaluate real organizations remains necessary before Practicum I; the instrumental case does not collapse, but it clearly weakens considerably over the decade.
HSP 2010.d: This survey course introduces the elements necessary for nonprofit organizations to achieve meaningful and lasting impact in their communities. Students will choose a single nonprofit to investigate throughout the semester, culminating in a report on the organization that includes suggestions for improving its impact.

r: HSP 2020 builds group-facilitation competence through experiential small-group work: recognizing interpersonal dynamics in real time, predicting how a group will move, and practicing leadership and facilitation skills live with peers. This is embodied, real-time interpersonal work; task-exposure research consistently places group facilitation and live leadership among the low-exposure categories, in contrast to writing and programming. AI can describe group-dynamics theory, but it cannot stand in a room and read a group's shifting affect, redirect a stalled discussion, or model facilitation under real interpersonal pressure. As one of two required alternatives, with HSP 2010, gating Practicum I, the course also carries prerequisite weight within the accredited program. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop this embodied facilitation skill through direct experiential practice is fully intact.

By 2031, AI tools may help students plan group activities or summarize group-dynamics theory in advance, but the graded competence, live facilitation, reading real-time interpersonal cues, adapting leadership style mid-session, remains an embodied, in-person activity outside AI's operating envelope. Task-exposure research's strongest negative associations are with exactly this kind of live interpersonal skill. The course's role as a required alternative prerequisite for Practicum I also holds across a catalog cycle; program sequencing does not restructure at the pace of model capability. The instrumental case is essentially unchanged from 24 months: AI reshapes how students might prepare conceptually, but the experiential core, practicing facilitation with real people in real time, is the entire point and is not delegable at all. The rating stays Low.

Even under a central-case ten-year capability trajectory, live group facilitation is not a task AI performs on a student's behalf; the embodied, real-time interpersonal core of the course sits at the protected end of the task-exposure spectrum, alongside other in-person leadership and counseling skills. Some preparatory content, theoretical background on group stages, conflict-resolution frameworks, may be increasingly AI-supported, but that does not touch the experiential requirement of practicing facilitation live with real peers. The required-alternative prerequisite role for Practicum I persists absent restructuring of the field-placement sequence. The honest uncertainty concerns how much conceptual scaffolding shifts to AI-assisted delivery, not whether developing embodied facilitation skill through direct practice remains instrumentally necessary. The rating holds Low, protected jointly by embodiment and the prerequisite architecture.
HSP 2020.d: Students will be introduced to the basic theories of small groups with experiential learning experiences to develop skills and strategies for effective group participation and leadership. The universality of feelings and concerns are shared to recognize the dynamics of interpersonal interaction, predict dynamics, accurately demonstrate effective leadership skills, and learn to facilitate the group process and interpersonal interactions in small-group situations.

The rating stays Low: preparatory theory content may increasingly be AI-assisted, but interviewing skill itself is not something a model builds for the student.

HSP 2030.d: This course familiarizes students with major theoretical approaches to counseling and psychotherapy and basic interview techniques. Emphasis will be placed on introducing behavioral intervention techniques common to most behavioral therapies. Students examine and practice effective interviewing skills and learn how to gather essential information about clients using the fundamental theories of counseling and psychotherapy.

But the content seeds later clinical and specialized human-services coursework within the accredited program, giving it a scaffolding role, and understanding family dynamics correctly matters for downstream client work. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this conceptual foundation directly, rather than relying on an AI summary, remains intact given its role feeding subsequent practice-oriented coursework.

The instrumental case shifts toward conceptual fluency needed to apply these frameworks correctly in later practicum and clinical coursework, and toward evaluating AI-generated family-systems analysis rather than simply consuming it. The course carries no GT-Pathways lock and does not appear in the explicit Practicum I prerequisite chain, so its institutional anchor is moderate rather than hard, though it remains part of the accredited program's theoretical core. Diffusion of AI explainer tools into human-services training is plausible on this horizon. The rating holds Low, resting more on the course's foundational role within the specialized curriculum than on strong task-exposure protection.

A decade out, AI explanation and comparison of family-systems frameworks will likely be thorough and readily available, substantially eroding the informational-transmission rationale for a review-style lecture course under a central-case trajectory. The theoretical grounding nonetheless continues to matter for students entering family-therapy-adjacent practice, and the moderate scaffolding role, feeding conceptual fluency into later specialized and clinical coursework, provides a real, if not absolute, counterweight. The rating rises to Medium, acknowledging that content delivery is increasingly automatable while the course's contributory role in preparing students for applied family-systems work persists across the sequence. The genuine uncertainty is how much the course shifts toward AI-assisted case analysis rather than lecture review, not whether some grounding in family-systems theory remains necessary before advanced practice.
HSP 2040.d: This class provides a brief review of family systems and the roles of family members in traditional and nontraditional families. The theoretical basis of family therapy modalities that serve as guidelines for therapy is described.

r: HSP 2070 prepares students for field placement: understanding what to expect, developing a resume, completing a mock interview, and defining personal learning goals tied to selecting an appropriate placement site. Resume drafting and interview preparation are squarely within the most AI-exposed task categories; observed-usage data show writing and career-preparation tasks are already heavily AI-assisted, and AI resume tools are common. But the course is the explicit, named prerequisite for Human Services Practicum I; a student cannot enter field placement without completing it, an institution-specific mandate no AI capability displaces. Defining individualized learning goals tied to a specific placement site also requires reflective judgment particular to the student. At 24 months the instrumental need to complete this required gateway is intact regardless of how automatable resume-writing has become.

By 2031, AI will draft polished resumes and coach mock interviews with real sophistication, essentially eliminating the execution rationale for those specific preparatory tasks. But HSP 2070 is not primarily valued for producing a resume artifact; it is the hard, named prerequisite gating entry to Practicum I, and that sequencing requirement does not relax within a catalog cycle regardless of how capable AI career-prep tools become. The instrumental case shifts almost entirely toward the gatekeeping function and toward the goal-setting and placement-selection judgment that remains the student's own responsibility. The rating holds Low: the content components are highly automatable, but the course's institutional role as the field-placement gate, and its status as critical prerequisite substrate for Practicum I, keeps it necessary.

A decade out, AI career-preparation tools will very likely handle resume drafting and interview rehearsal comprehensively under a central-case capability trajectory, and the applied-task automatability here is about as high as anywhere in this whole batch of courses. Yet the course's binding function is institutional rather than task-based: it remains the required prerequisite for Practicum I, and foundational scaffolding for the field-placement pathway caps the rating at Medium even as the underlying tasks become almost fully AI-deliverable. The rating rises to Medium primarily on task-exposure grounds, not because the prerequisite gate itself weakens. The uncertainty is whether the seminar itself gets substantially redesigned around AI-assisted preparation, not whether some required gateway to field placement persists in the central case through 2036.
HSP 2070.d: The Pre-Field Placement Seminar is designed to support student success in human services field placement experiences. Students will learn what to expect from and how to prepare for a field placement as well as develop a resume and participate in a mock interview process. Students will engage in an active learning process to begin to define their own learning goals and relate those goals to the selection of an appropriate field placement site.

Verification burden is also high, since a beginning practitioner's errors with real clients require an accountable, present supervisor. At 24 months the instrumental need for this embodied field experience is completely intact.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly assist practicum students with case documentation, resource look-up, or administrative tasks at the placement site, meaningfully augmenting the work. But the defining requirement, a student physically present at an agency, engaging real clients or organizational work under supervision, accumulating actual field-service hours, is untouched by that augmentation. Verification burden remains high because a novice's misjudgment with a real client carries real cost, and the accredited program's field-hour architecture does not restructure within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case is essentially unchanged from 24 months: AI may lighten the administrative load around the placement, but it cannot be the placement. The rating stays Low, anchored jointly by embodiment, supervision-dependent verification, and the field-hour requirement itself.

Even under an aggressive central-case ten-year capability trajectory, the requirement this course satisfies, physical, supervised presence in a human-service agency performing real client-facing or organizational work, is not a task AI performs on the student's behalf; embodiment is the entire premise of a practicum. Administrative and documentation support around the placement may automate further, and agencies may deploy more AI-assisted case tools by 2036, but that changes what the student does at the placement, not whether the placement itself remains required. The uncertainty concerns how field supervision and documentation evolve under ubiquitous AI tools, not whether direct supervised field experience remains instrumentally necessary for entry to human-services practice. The rating holds Low with high confidence, protected by embodiment, verification burden, and field-hour architecture together.
HSP 2080.d: This practicum provides a beginning field experience in a human service agency or setting. In addition to the field service hours, students participate in an interactive seminar that supports the effectiveness of student learning at the placement site and allows students to apply theoretical knowledge learned in the core human services curriculum to real life situations and experiences. Students participate in a variety of hands-on activities to develop clinical and/or nonprofit management skills depending on the nature of the placement.

r: HSP 2105 introduces trauma counseling foundations: evidence-based theories and models, the impact of trauma on cognitive, affective, behavioral, and neurological functioning, the centrality of the therapeutic relationship, multidisciplinary treatment teams, and the professional habits, cultural humility, healthy boundaries, self-care, needed when treating trauma-diagnosed clients. The conceptual survey elements map to updating-and-using-relevant-knowledge activities AI already explains fluently. But the therapeutic-relationship and boundary-setting content concerns high-stakes interpersonal judgment where a wrong application can retraumatize a vulnerable client, and verification burden stays high because such failures are often non-obvious to an inexperienced practitioner. Prerequisite entry via HSP 1020 situates the course within the program's trauma-specialization track. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this foundation under qualified instruction, rather than from an AI summary alone, remains intact.

By 2031, AI will competently explain trauma neurobiology and therapeutic-relationship theory, eroding the pure content-delivery function. But the jagged-frontier evidence is directly relevant here: outside a domain a learner has mastered, AI users are measurably less accurate and often overconfident, which is precisely the failure mode to avoid when internalizing boundary-setting and self-care practices for trauma-adjacent work, errors carry real client-harm potential and are hard to detect from the outside. That verification burden, combined with the course's specialized-track sequencing within the human-services curriculum, keeps a knowledgeable instructor and structured practice necessary. The instrumental case shifts toward critically evaluating AI-generated trauma-counseling content rather than simply receiving it. The rating holds Low across this horizon, anchored by verification burden more than task-exposure alone.

A decade out, AI delivery of trauma-counseling theory and neurobiological content will likely be extensive and well-developed under a central-case trajectory, substantially eroding the informational-transmission rationale for the course. The professional-judgment components, calibrating boundaries, recognizing the therapeutic relationship's role in treatment efficacy, functioning within a multidisciplinary team, retain real verification demands given the vulnerability of the client population, but the balance of the course plausibly shifts toward applying and checking AI-assisted trauma content rather than acquiring it from scratch. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting genuine erosion in content delivery while professional-judgment components and the course's role feeding the trauma-specialization track keep it from reaching High. The uncertainty concerns pedagogy under ubiquitous AI, not whether trauma-informed judgment remains necessary for this specialized practice track.
HSP 2105.d: In this class, students will develop a foundation for understanding trauma counseling utilizing various evidenced based theories and models. Students will be introduced to the impact of trauma on the cognitive, affective, behavioral, and neurological functioning of the individual. In addition, emphasis will be placed on the importance of the therapeutic relationship in the efficacy of treatment. Foci will include an overview of multidisciplinary teams in the treatment of trauma, as well as a focus on cultural humility, healthy boundaries, and self-care on the part of the professional treating clients diagnosed with trauma.

The applied task is convening real stakeholders, reading local power dynamics, and sustaining trust over time, work that resists remote automation at this horizon. There is no licensure lock, but the course sits inside the required human-services core, giving it a program-level accreditation floor that keeps the near-term instrumental need for direct organizing practice intact.

By 2031, AI drafting of coalition materials, needs assessments, and stakeholder communications will be considerably more capable and more embedded in agency workflows, and task-exposure research places writing and organizational-communication tasks among the more positively exposed categories. The accreditation floor for macro-practice content in the human-services curriculum continues to hold at the five-year mark. The rating rises to Medium as knowledge delivery erodes, while facilitation practice keeps it from climbing further.

Over a decade, capability trends suggest AI systems will competently draft organizing strategy, model stakeholder incentives, and simulate likely community responses, extending the automatable share of what this course teaches beyond documentation into strategic planning itself. Still, the instrumental case for a student to personally build organizing skill is not eliminated: convening and sustaining trust with real people over years is an embodied, presence-dependent task that resists even strong capability growth, and the accreditation-driven core requirement is unlikely to disappear within a single catalog cycle. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the strategic groundwork migrates to AI-assisted planning; the rating holds at Medium because the human-facilitation core remains, even as the surrounding analytical work becomes largely automatable by this horizon.
HSP 3000.d: This course reviews the theories and techniques of organizing groups to promote change in the community, and the role community organizers and other human service professionals play in community change. The course examines several distinct contexts for change and why and how change occurs or fails to occur. Strategies and tactics for promoting change are also included.

HSP 3010.d: Students are introduced to the etiology, assessment and treatment of mental health and substance use disorders. Students also examine therapeutic communication and counseling skills, trauma informed care and clinician self-care. Although designed to assist students in transitioning to the Masters of Science in Clinical Behavioral Health, Emphasis in Addiction Counseling, the course is available for anyone interested in addiction and mental health counseling.

Verification burden is severe, since a poorly delivered couples intervention can worsen relational harm and failures are often non-obvious in the room. At 24 months the instrumental need for the course is intact.

But the course's core is applied intervention skill: reading a couple's dynamic in real time, managing an emotionally charged room, and adjusting technique on the fly, work that remains stubbornly embodied and interpersonal. There is no hard licensure lock specific to this elective, only a program-level contribution to the human-services curriculum, so the institutional cap loosens earlier than for accredited core courses. The rating rises to Medium at this horizon: the theoretical scaffolding is increasingly AI-deliverable, but the supervised, real-time clinical-skill practice the course exists to build is not.

Over ten years, AI systems will plausibly be embedded as real-time coaching aids inside actual couples-therapy practice, consistent with the capability trend toward longer autonomous task horizons, further eroding the course's stand-alone knowledge-transmission role. The instrumental case for supervised skill-building persists, though: a practitioner learning to read relational dynamics and intervene appropriately under supervision is developing embodied judgment that differs from consuming AI-generated relationship guidance, and the jagged-frontier problem, users overtrusting AI outside its competence zone, argues for continued trained oversight in emotionally fraught clinical work.
